From circlize to ggcircos

Source: vignettes/from-circlize.Rmd
from-circlize.Rmd
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ggcircos)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

The honest framing

circlize is the most capable circular-plotting package in R. It has more geometry types, more options, and a decade of accumulated edge-case handling. If you need a ideogram with cytogenetic bands, use circlize.

ggcircos exists for the things circlize structurally cannot do. circlize paints into its own canvas: the figure is a side effect of a sequence of drawing calls, not an object. So you cannot facet a circlize figure, you cannot drive its colours with a ggplot2 scale and get a legend, you cannot compose two of them with patchwork, and you cannot save one and add a layer next week. ggcircos keeps the circular layout but hands the drawing back to ggplot2, because the layout is just a table of angles.

This vignette maps the API and shows the three things you can do here and cannot do there.

The same picture, two ways 

mat <- round(cor(mtcars)[1:6, 1:6], 2)

circlize::chordDiagram(as.matrix(mat), symmetric = TRUE,
                       diffHeight = 0.02,
                       annotationTrack = "grid",
                       preAllocateTracks = list(list(track.height = 0.08)))
# the labels live in the annotation track's panel function, querying the
# canvas for each cell's position -- this is the part with no ggplot2 analogue
circlize::circos.trackPlotRegion(track.index = 1, panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    xlim <- circlize::get.cell.meta.data("xlim")
    circlize::circos.text(mean(xlim), 0.04,
                          circlize::get.cell.meta.data("sector.index"),
                          cex = 0.7, facing = "outside")
})

circlize: the same 6x6 correlation matrix. 

p <- ggcircos(mat, order = "hclust") +
    geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick",
                         midpoint = 0, name = "r") +
    geom_node_arc() +
    geom_node_text()
print(p)

ggcircos: the same matrix, with the legend for free.

The circlize call is one line; the labels are two more, because circlize draws them through a panel function that queries its own canvas. The ggcircos call is the layout plus four layers, and the legend came free.

The API map

circlize ggcircos note
chordDiagram(mat) ggcircos(mat) + geom_chord() matrix input is native
chordDiagramFromDataframe(df) ggcircos(df, nodes = , sectors = ) a link table is the general form
circos.initialize(factors = ) sectors = "col" a sector is a group of nodes
circos.track(...) ggcircos(tracks = c(...)) + geom_track(...) bands are declared up front
circos.text(...) geom_node_text() / geom_track(geom = "text")
circos.axis(...) geom_track_axis(band = , limits = ) limits is required
circos.link(...) geom_chord(type = "line")
circos.par(...) theme_circos() + layer arguments there is no global state
get.cell.meta.data(...) layout_nodes() / layout_links() the canvas query became a table
circos.genomicTrack(df) geom_track(aes(xmin = start, xmax = end), domain = len) a feature is a range, not a point
circos.genomicRect(...) geom_track(geom = "tile") with xmin/xmax no separate geom needed
circos.genomicAxis(...) geom_track_axis(limits = c(0, chr_length)) numeric ticks, not chr1:1,000 labels
a threshold line geom_track_hline(band = , value = ) value is a track value, not an angle
circos.nested(...) not supported compose two plots instead (see below)

Three translation rules cover most of the rest. circlize’s global state (circos.par, the current track index) becomes explicit arguments on the layer that uses them. circlize’s track.height becomes a named width in tracks = c(name = width), because the bands must be declared before any layer can refer to them. And circlize’s per-call xlim/ylim on a genomicTrack() becomes the domain/origin pair: domain names the node column holding each chromosome’s length, so a 100 Mb chromosome and a 5 Mb contig each fill their own arc instead of being forced onto one scale.

Two entries deserve a word. circos.genomicAxis() labels a chromosome in chr1:1,000,000 form; geom_track_axis() is a plain numeric ruler, so you give it limits = c(0, 4000) and read the numbers as base pairs – turning that into ideogram-style tick text is not something this package does yet. And circos.nested() draws one circle inside another sharing a common sector; here the two are separate plots, which is the point of the model: put them side by side with patchwork, or facet one plot by group.

What only ggcircos can do

Facets

facet_wrap() has two meanings here, and which one you get depends on whether you pass by =.

Shared ring (the default). Four samples of the same eight variables become four panels that share one node ring – the chords split per sample, the ring does not. This is circlize’s four canvases made one call, but every panel keeps the same node order.

mk <- function(s) {
    m <- matrix(runif(8 * 8), 8, 8)
    m <- (m + t(m)) / 2
    diag(m) <- 0
    d <- as.data.frame(as.table(m))
    names(d) <- c("from", "to", "r")
    d$sample <- s
    d
}
links <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, mk))

p_facet <- ggcircos(links, order = "hclust") +
    geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
    geom_node_arc() +
    geom_node_text() +
    facet_wrap(~ sample)
#> ℹ Dropped 32 self-links (`from == to`); use `self_loops = TRUE`
#> to draw them.
print(p_facet)

Shared ring: the chords split per sample; every panel draws the same node ring in the same order.

The build proves the structure: one data frame per layer, each carrying a PANEL column — not one drawing per panel.

b <- ggplot_build(p_facet)
c(panels = length(unique(b$layout$layout$PANEL)),
  layers = length(b$data),
  rows_per_layer = vapply(b$data, nrow, integer(1)))
#>          panels          layers rows_per_layer1 rows_per_layer2 rows_per_layer3 
#>               4               3             224              32              32

One ring per group (by =). When each panel should have its own nodes and its own ordering, name a node-table column with by =. The layout is then built once per group. Here the samples do not even share nodes.

set.seed(1)
nodes <- data.frame(
  id  = paste0("g", 1:10),
  grp = rep(c("sample A", "sample B"), each = 5),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
links <- data.frame(
  from = c("g1", "g2", "g3", "g6", "g7", "g8"),
  to   = c("g2", "g3", "g5", "g7", "g8", "g10"),
  grp  = rep(c("sample A", "sample B"), each = 3),
  w    = runif(6, 0.3, 0.9),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ggcircos(links, nodes = nodes, by = "grp", weight = "w") +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = w)) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text() +
  facet_wrap(~ grp)

One ring per sample: each panel has its own node set and its own layout, from a single ggcircos(by = ) call.

A link belongs to the panel named in its own grp column; a node id may repeat across groups, since each panel is laid out independently. Without a link column, a link is filed under the group of its two ends, and one that spans groups is dropped.

Tracks work too, and each panel places its own: a row is put at the angle its group gives that node, so the same id can sit in a different place in different rings. The track data therefore needs the grouping column as well.

trk <- data.frame(
  id  = c(paste0("g", 1:5), paste0("g", 6:10)),
  grp = rep(c("sample A", "sample B"), each = 5),
  gc  = runif(10, 0.25, 0.75),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ggcircos(links, nodes = nodes, by = "grp", weight = "w",
         tracks = c(gc = 0.22)) +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = w)) +
  geom_track(data = trk, aes(x = gc), node = id, band = "gc",
             fill = "steelblue", colour = NA) +
  geom_track_axis(band = "gc", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ grp)

Tracks on a by = plot: each panel places its own track, and the axis stands before that panel’s first node.

Scales and legends

The fill of a ribbon is a mapped aesthetic, so the whole ggplot2 scale system applies — including legends, guides, and scale_*_manual():

ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust") +
    geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick",
                         midpoint = 0, name = "correlation") +
    geom_node_arc() + geom_node_text()

A diverging scale drives the ribbons and the legend.

Composition

A ggcircos plot is a grob like any other, so it composes:

p_a <- ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust") +
    geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) + geom_node_arc() + theme_circos()
vals <- data.frame(id = rep(colnames(mtcars), each = 3),
                   value = runif(33))
p_b <- ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust", tracks = c(v = 0.25)) +
    geom_track(data = vals, aes(x = value), node = id, band = "v") +
    geom_node_arc() + theme_circos()
p_a + p_b + patchwork::plot_annotation(title = "two rings, one grammar")

A chord diagram and a track diagram side by side.

Self-loops

circlize draws a self-link as a small loop folded toward the centre. The same is available here: pass self_loops = TRUE and a from == to row becomes a loop on its own node, rather than being dropped. Like circlize’s, it folds inward instead of running the full way round – a full turn would sit on top of the node and stop reading as a link.

nodes <- data.frame(id = c("a", "b", "c", "d"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
links <- data.frame(
  from = c("a", "b", "b", "c", "a"),
  to   = c("b", "b", "c", "d", "d"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ggcircos(links, nodes = nodes, self_loops = TRUE) +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = self_loop)) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text()

A self-loop on node b, drawn as a loop folded toward the centre. The other links are ordinary chords.

loop_depth (default 0.5) says how far the loop folds toward the centre: 0 would not fold at all, 1 would reach it. A narrow node gets a shallow loop automatically, so several self-loops on a crowded ring do not pile into the middle.

One node, several radii

Sometimes the same entity belongs on the ring more than once – a protein in two interaction networks, a feature present in two assemblies. The nodes table may list an id several times, once per radius, and the r column says which. The layers are stacked above one another on the same place of the ring, and each keeps its own links.

nodes <- data.frame(
  id = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"),
  r = c(1, 1.45, 1, 1.45, 1, 1.45),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
links <- data.frame(
  from = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c"),
  to = c("b", "b", "c", "c", "a"),
  from_r = c(1, 1.45, 1, 1.45, 1),
  to_r = c(1, 1.45, 1, 1.45, 1.45),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ggcircos(links, nodes = nodes) +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = from_r), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_arc()

One node id at two radii: the inner ring and the outer ring are the same node, with their own links.

The inner and the outer ring are the same three nodes, one layer each: the layers share their place on the ring and stack outwards, and each keeps its own links. The chords are drawn translucent here so both layers stay visible.

A link says which layer it lives on with from_r / to_r. A link whose end does not name a radius is an error when the node has several layers – the package lists the radii rather than picking one.

What ggcircos does not do yet

  • Self-loops (from == to) are drawn only with self_loops = TRUE; by default they are dropped with a message.
  • No label collision avoidance; rotate labels or shorten them.
  • No track type beyond col, bar, area, boxplot, violin, density, point, tile, text.
  • No angular axis (the circle has no “hours” scale).
  • No ideogram / cytogenetic band knowledge — circlize ships the data, we do not.
  • No interactive output. plotly::ggplotly() will not crash on a ggcircos plot, but it will not render the chords either.
  • A continuous fill is quantised into batches of at most 8/255 colour steps to keep the grob count low.

These are choices, not oversights: the package is one grammar, not a feature race.

If you are coming from circlize

  1. Replace chordDiagram(mat) with ggcircos(mat) + geom_chord() and add geom_node_arc() / geom_node_text() — the annotation ring is a layer now, not a side effect.
  2. Move each circos.track() into geom_track(), and declare its band in ggcircos(tracks = c(name = width)) first.
  3. Keep the sector concept: circos.initialize(factors = ) becomes nodes = plus sectors = "col".
  4. Expect to set limits yourself on geom_track_axis(); ggcircos will not guess the range of another layer’s data.
  5. Then try the thing you could not do before: facet_wrap(~ sample).
